questions.q: What is the actual difference between 'the incident is fixed' and 'the platform is ready for next season'?
options: There is no difference — they mean the same thing
The incident being fixed addresses one specific bug; being ready for next season means deliberately reducing the chance and blast radius of a future one
Being ready for next season only means buying more hardware
The incident was never actually fixed
questions.explain: Closing one incident and hardening the platform going forward are two different milestones, and this lesson scopes the second one deliberately.

questions.q: What are the three workstreams this lesson scopes the next phase into?
options: Marketing, sales, and finance
The dashboard/alert audit, the capacity question, and documentation and validation
Rewriting the application, replacing Kubernetes, and switching cloud providers
Hiring, budgeting, and recruiting
questions.explain: Each workstream has its own owner and its own definition of done: a reviewed audit list, an agreed capacity number, and a durable document.

questions.q: Why can't the capacity question simply wait until the dashboard/alert audit is finished?
options: Because Casey and Dana already have opinions about capacity and that conversation is going to happen on its own timeline regardless
Because the audit will never actually finish
Because capacity isn't actually a real concern for Driftwood
Because Theo has no opinion on the matter
questions.explain: Real planning doesn't get the luxury of a tidy sequence — the capacity conversation needs to be scoped as its own workstream rather than absorbed as an afterthought.

questions.q: Which of the following is explicitly named as OUT of scope for this next phase?
options: Reviewing dashboard panels for hidden averages
A full multi-region active-active redesign of the existing architecture
Agreeing on an autoscaling ceiling
Documenting the fix and the new dashboard panel
questions.explain: This phase hardens the existing AKS-plus-secondary-cloud architecture — it deliberately does not redesign it from scratch.

questions.q: Why does Theo structure the next phase into three NAMED workstreams instead of one general 'harden the platform' backlog item?
options: Because naming things is a company policy at Driftwood
Because each workstream has a genuinely different kind of 'done,' and a vague backlog item has no way to tell when it's actually finished
Because Casey insisted on exactly three items
Because it looks better in a slide deck
questions.explain: A reviewed audit list, an agreed capacity number, and a durable document are three different, checkable outcomes — a single vague backlog item couldn't distinguish between them.
